name: Abhinanda (Gauḍa Abhinanda)
summary: Kashmiri author to whom the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha is ascribed.

name: Abhinavagupta
summary: The central figure of Kashmirian non-dual Śaivism: author of the Tantrāloka, Tantrasāra, Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa, Mālinīślokavārttika, the two commentaries on the Īśvarapratyabhijñā, the Paramārthasāra, Gītārthasaṅgraha, devotional hymns, and of the Abhinavabhāratī and Locana in aesthetics. He integrated Trika, Kula, Krama, Spanda and Pratyabhijñā under the four upāyas.

scholarly.text: c. 975-1025 CE; dated works: Kramastotra (Laukika 66, c. 990/91), Bhairavastava (68, c. 992/93), Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (90, c. 1014/15)

realization_account.text: The Tantrāloka describes one born of a union of parents absorbed in the Kaula state as 'yoginībhū', by nature a vessel of knowledge, Rudra himself (TĀ 29.162-163), a description the tradition applies to Abhinavagupta. Later Kashmiri tradition relates that he entered the Bhairava cave near Bīrwa with many disciples and did not return (oral legend; low confidence).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Teacher ids tch:induraja and tch:bhatta-tauta (poetics, dramaturgy) belong to U31.
alt_summary: Author of the Gītārthasaṅgraha on the Kashmir recension of the Gītā.

name: Acyutaprekṣa
summary: The ascetic at Uḍupi from whom Madhva took renunciation; the Sumadhvavijaya calls him Acyutapramati. In the tradition's account his ascetic line had come under the teaching of māyā, and he later accepted his disciple's doctrine.
notes: The earlier names of his line (the 'Haṃsa paramparā' back to Nārāyaṇa as Haṃsa and Brahmā) are not listed; see lin:dvaita notes.

name: Adhokṣaja Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Pejavara maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Agastya
summary: In the Vīraśaiva tradition, the sage to whom Reṇuka taught the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi on the Malaya mountain (SSM 1.29; ch. 4–5).
notes: Contribution of U20 to a shared registry entity (Agastya is owned elsewhere).
alt_summary: In the Rāmāyaṇa the sage Agastya teaches Rāma the Āditya Hṛdaya before the final battle (Yuddhakāṇḍa 105/107).

In the Purāṇas the sage who, pilgrimaging with Lopāmudrā, receives the Lalitopākhyāna from Hayagrīva, and who in the Kāśī Khaṇḍa teaches Lopāmudrā the inner tīrthas (SkP 4.1.6.28-45); he also cursed Indradyumna to become the elephant Gajendra.

name: Aghoraśiva
notes: Contribution from U08.
summary: Saiddhāntika ācārya of Cidambaram whose ritual manual (Kriyākramadyotikā, 1157/58) became the standard for Tamil Śaiva temple and domestic ritual; he also wrote commentaries on the Mṛgendravṛtti, the Sarvajñānottara and works of Sadyojyoti and Bhoja.

name: Ajagaṇṇa
summary: Muktāyakka's brother, a hidden devotee whose death occasions her meeting with Allama.

name: Akka Mahādēvi
summary: Akka Mahādēvi (Mahādēviyakka) of Uḍutaḍi, the woman saint who took Śiva as Cennamallikārjuna for her only husband, left a royal household, wandered clad only in her hair, was examined by Allama at Kalyāṇa and ended at Kadaḷi on Śrīśaila; her vacanas of bridal devotion and fearless renunciation are the tradition's great witness to women's spiritual equality.

realization_account.text: Devoted from childhood to Cennamallikārjuna, she refused (or left) the king Kauśika, renounced even clothing, was tested and acknowledged by Allama and the śaraṇas at Kalyāṇa, and attained union in the Kadaḷi forest of Śrīśaila.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Whether she was married to Kauśika differs between sources; recorded as the sources' variance.

name: Akkamma
summary: A woman vacanakāra of the śaraṇa circle whose vacanas are included in the modern collections of the women śaraṇas; details of her life are not recorded here.

name: Akkanāgamma
summary: Basava's sister (Nāgalāmbike), mother of Cennabasava and a vacanakāra.

name: Akṛtavraṇa
summary: One of Romaharṣaṇa's disciples in both lists (VP 3.6.17; BhP 12.7.5), of the Kāśyapa lineage (VP 3.6.18 counts 'Kāśyapa' among the makers of saṃhitās; BhP 12.7.7 calls Akṛtavraṇa a disciple of Rāma Jāmadagnya).

name: Akṣobhya Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva, pontiff after Mādhava Tīrtha, and teacher of Jayatīrtha. The Mādhva tradition records his debate with the Advaitin Vidyāraṇya on 'tat tvam asi', with Vedānta Deśika as arbiter, and a verse it ascribes to Deśika declaring Akṣobhya the victor; the Advaita tradition does not accept this account.
notes: See dsp:aksobhya-vidyaranya-debate.

name: al-Bīrūnī
alt_names: Abū Rayḥān Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Bīrūnī
summary: Khwārazmian scholar who learned Sanskrit in India and rendered a Pātañjala yoga text with a commentary into Arabic (Kitāb Pātanǧal). He was not a member of the tradition; he is listed under this lineage only as the translator of its text.

name: Alarka
summary: Youngest son of Madālasā and King Ṛtadhvaja (Kuvalayāśva); raised as a king, he received his mother's ring-instruction and, when defeated in war, went to Dattātreya, learned yoga and renounced (MkP 25-44).
alt_summary: A royal sage who first sought to conquer the mind and senses with arrows and then learned that they are conquered only by yoga (Anugītā 14.30).

name: Alaśiṅga Bhaṭṭa
notes: Role: commentator. Date not established.
summary: Commentator on the Sātvata Saṃhitā.

name: Allama Prabhu
summary: Allama Prabhu (Prabhudēva), the mystic of the void (śūnya, bayalu) whose enigmatic vacanas, signed Guhēśvara, test every attainment; in the Śūnyasampādane he presides over the Anubhava Maṇṭapa on the 'throne of the void' and examines Basava, Cennabasava, Siddharāma, Akka Mahādēvi, Muktāyakka and Gorakṣa.

realization_account.text: Harihara: a temple drummer of Baḷḷigāve who, grieving the death of Kāmalate, came upon a buried shrine where the yogi Animiṣa placed a liṅga in his hand and passed away, and he awoke. Cāmarasa: Śiva's own descent, unmoved by Māyā sent by Pārvatī, whose body passes untouched by Gorakṣa's sword. He ended in Kadaḷi at Śrīśaila, merging into the liṅga.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Ambigara Cauḍayya
summary: The ferryman śaraṇa whose vacanas, signed with his own name, attack hypocrisy, ritualism and the pride of learning.

name: Ānanda (father of Somānanda)
summary: Son of Aruṇāditya and father of Somānanda (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.120).
notes: Id disambiguated from tch:ananda (the Buddha's attendant).

name: Ānandabhaṭṭa (Bhaṭṭānanda)
summary: Author of the Vijñānakaumudī on the Vijñāna Bhairava; its opening honours Somānanda, Bhūtirāja, Utpala, Lakṣmaṇagupta and Abhinavagupta.

name: Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Tātparyaprakāśa commentary on the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

name: Ānandagiri (Ānandajñāna)
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on many of Śaṅkara's works, including the Gītābhāṣya.

name: Anantadeva (author of the Padacandrikā)
summary: Author of the Padacandrikā, a short commentary on the Yoga Sūtra dedicated to Śiva.
notes: Whether he is identical with other authors named Anantadeva (e.g. the 17th-c. Mīmāṃsaka) is not established here; id disambiguated for that reason.

name: Anantaśaktipāda
summary: Commentator on the Vātūlanāthasūtra.

name: Anasūyā
summary: Ascetic wife of the sage Atri, honoured for her austerities, who teaches Sītā the dharma of the devoted wife (Rāmāyaṇa 2.117–119).

name: Animiṣayya
summary: The 'unblinking' yogi who, in Harihara's account, placed the liṅga in Allama's hand in a buried shrine and passed away, awakening him.

name: Aniruddha (Sāṃkhya commentator)
summary: Author of the earliest known commentary (vṛtti) on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra.

name: Annambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkasaṅgraha and its Dīpikā, the most widely used primer of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, written 'for the easy understanding of beginners'; tradition makes him a scholar from the Andhra country who worked in Vārāṇasī.

name: Apāntaratamas
summary: Born of Nārāyaṇa's word, the teacher of the Vedas (vedācārya), called by some Prācīnagarbha; Vyāsa says he himself was Apāntaratamas in a former birth (12.337.38–61).

name: Appaṇṇācārya
summary: Disciple of Rāghavendra Tīrtha to whom the tradition ascribes the Rāghavendra-stotra recited by devotees.

name: Arjuna (Pārtha, Dhanaṃjaya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The third Pāṇḍava, the archer, whose refusal to fight his kinsmen occasions the Gītā; he declares himself Kṛṣṇa's disciple and takes refuge in him (2.7), receives the divine eye and the vision of the universal form (11.8ff), and after the war asks Kṛṣṇa to repeat the teaching (Anugītā 14.16).

name: Aruṇāditya
summary: Son of Varṣāditya in Somānanda's lineage (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.119).

name: Asita Devala
summary: Sage named in the Gītā among those who proclaim Kṛṣṇa supreme (10.13); he teaches Nārada the five eternal elements with time as the sixth (12.267.1–6), and learns equanimity from the yogin Jaigīṣavya (12.222; 9.49).

name: Aṣṭāvakra
summary: A sage born bent in eight places by his father Kahoḍa's curse; as a boy he defeated Bandin at Janaka's court (Mahābhārata 3.132-134). The Aṣṭāvakra Gītā presents him as Janaka's teacher of non-dual knowledge.

name: Āsuri
alt_names: the brahmin of the Āsuri clan (āsurisagotra)

realization_account.text: A brahmin devoted to sacrifice for a thousand years; Kapila asked him three times, at thousand-year intervals, whether he delighted in the householder's life; the third time he answered that he did not, renounced, and became Kapila's disciple (Māṭhara). His dispassion arose from the presence of the supreme sage (Yuktidīpikā on SK 43).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Kapila's disciple and Pañcaśikha's teacher (SK 70). The commentaries describe him as a brahmin of the Āsuri clan who renounced householder life after Kapila's repeated questioning. A person named Āsuri also appears in Vedic ritual literature; identity with the Sāṃkhya Āsuri is uncertain.
alt_summary: Named in the Mokṣadharma as the teacher of Pañcaśikha in Kapila's line (12.211.10).

name: Ātmasukha
summary: Recalled as author of the Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā on the Laghu Yoga Vāsiṣṭha.

name: Atri
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Samūrtārcanādhikaraṇa.

name: Āvaṭya
summary: Sage, 'bearer of a body' (tanudhara), who questions Jaigīṣavya in YBh 3.18 about whether the happiness of contentment too belongs to suffering.

name: Aviddhakarṇa
summary: Early Naiyāyika known only from citations in Buddhist works (Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha and Kamalaśīla's commentary), among them arguments for Īśvara.
notes: Known only through opponents' reports; details unverified.

name: Āydakki Lakkamma
summary: Mārayya's wife, a vacanakāra remembered for sending back rice gathered beyond the day's need, teaching that kāyaka and dāsōha exclude hoarding.

name: Āydakki Mārayya
summary: The śaraṇa who lived by gleaning rice grains fallen in the market; his vacana declares that kāyaka is Kailāsa.

name: Bāl Gaṅgādhar Tilak
summary: Scholar and political leader whose Gītā Rahasya (1915) argues that the Gītā teaches action (karma-yoga) by the enlightened rather than renunciation.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa
summary: Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theologian, author of the Gītābhūṣaṇa (and the Govinda-bhāṣya on the Brahma Sūtra).

name: Bālarāma Udāsīna
summary: Modern scholar of the Udāsīna order to whom the Vidvattoṣiṇī on the Tattvakaumudī is ascribed.

name: Bali
summary: In the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha (5.22-29), the asura king who remembers his father Virocana's teaching on the realm beyond the worlds, inquires, and attains self-knowledge while continuing to rule.
alt_summary: The defeated Daitya king who tells Indra that Time takes and gives all, and bears his fall without grief (12.216–218).

name: Basava
summary: Basava (Basavaṇṇa, Basaveśvara), minister at the Kalacuri court of Bijjala in Kalyāṇa, the central figure of the twelfth-century śaraṇa movement; his vacanas, signed Kūḍalasaṅgamadēva, teach devotion, humility before devotees, work as worship, sharing, and the equality of all who wear the liṅga.

realization_account.text: Born to a brāhmaṇa family, he refused the sacred-thread initiation, took refuge at Kūḍalasaṅgama where Śiva as Saṅgamadēva became his lord, and was sent to Kalyāṇa, where as treasurer and minister he served the devotees, gathered the śaraṇas and founded the Anubhava Maṇṭapa; after the upheaval that followed an intercaste marriage among the śaraṇas he returned to Kūḍalasaṅgama and became one with the liṅga there.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Parents in the hagiographies: Mādarasa and Mādalāmbike (moderate). In the Pañcācārya account he is a great devotee within an older stream; in the śaraṇa account the founder. A Jaina narrative of Bijjala's reign gives a hostile account of these events (low confidence).

name: Bharadvāja
summary: Seer who questions Bhṛgu in the Mokṣadharma (12.175–185), raising doubts about the existence of a living self in a body made of elements.

name: Bharata (Rāma's brother)
summary: Rāma's brother, who refuses the throne and rules as Rāma's regent; Rāma's teachings on impermanence and kingship are addressed to him (2.100–105).
notes: Disambiguated from Bharata Muni (tch:bharata-muni).

name: Bhārgava (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Bhāsarvajña
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyasāra and its auto-commentary Nyāyabhūṣaṇa, known for independent positions: only three means of knowledge, and liberation as the cessation of pain qualified by the experience of eternal bliss. A Śaiva of Pāśupata orientation.
notes: The Ratnaṭīkā on the Pāśupata Gaṇakārikā is also attributed to him (attribution recalled, not checked).

name: Bhāskara
summary: Bhedābheda Vedāntin credited with a Gītā commentary defending the combination of knowledge and works.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Bhāskara (author of the Śivasūtravārttika)
summary: Kashmiri teacher, 'son of Bhaṭṭa Divākara', who wrote the Śivasūtravārttika on the teaching received from Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa, giving an account of the Śiva Sūtra's revelation and lineage that differs from Kṣemarāja's.

scholarly.text: c. 10th-11th c. CE; relation to Kṣemarāja debated

notes: Id disambiguated from tch:bhaskara (the Bhedābheda Vedāntin) and tch:bhaskarakantha.

name: Bhāskarakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmiri Paṇḍit, author of the Mokṣopāyaṭīkā and (outside U06) of the Bhāskarī commentary on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī.
alt_summary: 18th-century Kashmiri scholar, author of the Bhāskarī on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī and of a commentary on the Mokṣopāya (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha); identified by many with the Rājānaka Bhāskara who rendered Lal Ded's vākhs into Sanskrit verse.
notes: Identification with the Lallāvākyāni translator is low confidence.

name: Bhāskararāya
summary: In this unit: author of the Guptavatī commentary on the Devī Māhātmya (his Śrīvidyā works belong to U23).

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa
summary: Author of the Stavacintāmaṇi, a hymn to Śiva quoted in Utpaladeva's commentary on the Śivadṛṣṭi as the work of a 'former teacher' (pūrvaguru).

name: Bhāvāgaṇeśa
summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu; author of the Tattvayāthārthyadīpana on the Tattvasamāsa.
alt_summary: Pupil of Vijñānabhikṣu and author of a Dīpikā on the Yoga Sūtra that condenses his teacher's Vārttika.

name: Bhavānanda Siddhāntavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Bhavānandī sub-commentary on the Dīdhiti.

name: Bhīma (Bhīmasena)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Second Pāṇḍava; argues for artha and action against Yudhiṣṭhira's forbearance (3.34; 12.10); instructed by Hanumān on the ages and the duties of the varṇas (3.147–150).

name: Bhīmakavi
summary: Kannada poet who rendered the Basava Purāṇa into ṣaṭpadi verse in 1369.

name: Bhīṣma (Devavrata, Gāṅgeya)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Son of Śaṃtanu and Gaṅgā, the Kuru elder who vowed celibacy; granted mastery over the moment of his death, he lies on a bed of arrows waiting for the sun's northern course (6.114.89–98) and instructs Yudhiṣṭhira in Rājadharma, Āpaddharma and Mokṣadharma (Śāntiparvan) and in the Anuśāsana, including the thousand names of Viṣṇu; at death his self, restrained in all the openings, pierces the crown and rises to heaven (13.154.5).

name: Bhoja
summary: Paramāra king of Dhārā and polymath, author of the Rājamārtaṇḍa, a concise vṛtti on the Yoga Sūtra; its introductory verses praise him for works on grammar, on the Pātañjala (yoga) and on medicine.
notes: Contribution from U08; registry id shared with U10 (Rājamārtaṇḍa).
alt_summary: Paramāra king of Dhārā, author of a Siddhānta ritual manual (Siddhāntasārapaddhati) and of the doctrinal Tattvaprakāśa, besides works in other fields.

name: Bhṛgu
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes several adhikāras on temple ritual (Kriyādhikāra, Khilādhikāra, Prakīrṇādhikāra and others).
alt_summary: Ancient seer who answers Bharadvāja on creation, the elements, the self, the varṇas and the āśramas (12.175–185).

name: Bhuśuṇḍa
summary: The ancient crow living on a wish-fulfilling tree on a peak of Meru, who tells Vasiṣṭha how contemplation of the breath (prāṇa-cintā) made him outlive many world-ages (Mokṣopāya 6.14-27; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha). The Rāmcaritmānas's Kāk Bhuśuṇḍi is a related figure.

realization_account.text: Resting in the Self through contemplation of the breath, he remains unaffected by the dissolutions of the worlds he has witnessed.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Bhūtirāja
summary: A Kashmiri Śaiva teacher named among Abhinavagupta's teachers and praised by Ānandabhaṭṭa (Vijñānakaumudī, opening) with Somānanda and Utpala among those who descended to restore the Śaiva teaching.
notes: Subject taught to Abhinavagupta not verified here.

name: Bodhya
summary: A tranquil sage who, questioned by King Nahuṣa, names six teachers: Piṅgalā, the osprey, the snake, the bee, the arrow-maker and the maiden (Mahābhārata 12.171.57-61).

name: Brahmānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Advaita scholar who wrote the Laghucandrikā on Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaitasiddhi, answering the Mādhva Rāmācārya's Taraṅgiṇī.

name: Brahmaṇya Tīrtha
summary: The ascetic of Abbūr who gave renunciation to Vyāsatīrtha; the colophons of the Nyāyāmṛta name Vyāsatīrtha as his disciple.
notes: Discipleship stated in the Nyāyāmṛta colophons checked against the Devanāgarī e-text in sources_raw/raw_etexts/vedAntam/dvaitam (github.com/sanskrit/raw_etexts); numbering follows that copy and may differ in other editions.

name: Bṛhaspati
summary: Preceptor of the gods; he officiates at Uparicara Vasu's sacrifice (12.323) and questions Prajāpati Manu on the highest knowledge (12.194).

name: Buddhamitra
summary: Buddhist teacher of Vasubandhu according to Paramārtha's Life of Vasubandhu, which tells that he was defeated in debate by the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa before a king at Ayodhyā; Vasubandhu is said to have answered with his (lost) Paramārthasaptati.
notes: Lineage assignment follows the biography's setting; verify.

name: Cāmarasa
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet at the court of Dēvarāya II of Vijayanagara, author of the Prabhuliṅgalīle on Allama Prabhu.

name: Candramati
summary: Author of the Daśapadārthaśāstra, a Vaiśeṣika treatise of ten categories preserved only in Xuanzang's Chinese translation.
notes: The alternative name form is recalled with low confidence.

name: Candrānanda
summary: Author of the Vṛtti on the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra that transmits the older recension of the sūtras.

name: Cennabasava
summary: Cennabasava (Cennabasavaṇṇa), Basava's nephew, honoured as the master of ṣaṭsthala doctrine; his vacanas are signed Kūḍalacennasaṅgamadēva, and after the Kalyāṇa upheaval he led the śaraṇas with the vacana manuscripts to Uḷavi.

realization_account.text: Son of Basava's sister Akkanāgamma; the Śūnyasampādane has Allama acknowledge his knowledge of the sthalas, and he gives liṅga-initiation to Siddharāma; he attained union at Uḷavi.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Cēnnās Nārāyaṇan Nampūtirippāṭ
summary: Kerala brahmin of the Cēnnās family — hereditary tantris of the Guruvāyūr temple — and author of the Tantrasamuccaya, the standard manual of Kerala temple ritual.

name: Cinnambhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Tarkabhāṣāprakāśikā on Keśava Miśra's Tarkabhāṣā.

name: Cūḍālā
summary: Queen of Mālava who attained self-knowledge by her own inquiry and powers through breath-discipline; unable to teach her husband Śikhidhvaja as herself, she came to him in the forest disguised as the young brāhmaṇa Kumbha and led him to realization (Mokṣopāya 6.81-114; Yoga Vāsiṣṭha Nirvāṇa, pūrvārdha).

realization_account.text: Through daily inquiry into what the self is she found the Self and 'shone' so that her husband remarked on her changed radiance (MU 6.82-83 'cūḍālā-prabodha', 'cūḍālātmalābha').
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Daivarāti Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā instructed by Yājñavalkya in the Mokṣadharma (12.298–306).
notes: Whether he is the Upaniṣadic Janaka (tch:janaka) is not asserted.

name: Dāruka
summary: A gaṇa dear to Śiva, paired with Reṇuka among the pramathas; Reṇuka's leap over him in Śiva's assembly is the occasion of Reṇuka's descent (SSM 2.27; 3.67–77).
notes: In Pañcācārya yuga-lists Dāruka is also named among the ācāryas of an earlier age (low confidence).

name: Dattātreya
summary: Son of Atri and Anasūyā, counted the sixth avatāra in the Bhāgavata (1.3.11: he taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others); Yadu and the Haihayas gained yogic powers from him (2.7.4). The tradition identifies him with the unnamed avadhūta who teaches King Yadu his twenty-four teachers (Bhāgavata 11.7-9), and ascribes to him the Avadhūta Gītā and the Jīvanmukta Gītā. Revered as the ādiguru of the Datta tradition and in the Nāth lineages.

realization_account.text: Son of Atri and Anasūyā (a portion of Viṣṇu; in some accounts of the Trimūrti), the sixth avatāra who 'taught ānvīkṣikī to Alarka, Prahlāda and others' (BhP 1.3.11); an avadhūta who hid his yoga under outward impurity (MkP 16-19); in the Bhāgavata he tells of his twenty-four teachers (BhP 11.7-9, U06).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The avadhūta yogin of the Purāṇas whose teaching to Alarka (MkP 37-43) is the Mārkaṇḍeya's yoga: discrimination of self and body, posture, breath, dhāraṇā, obstacles, powers, Oṃ and the signs of death.

name: Devabodha
summary: Early commentator on the Mahābhārata (Jñānadīpikā).

name: Devahūti
summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of the sage Kardama and mother of Kapila; the questioner of the Kapila Gītā, who asks for a devotion suited to her and attains liberation.

realization_account.text: Following her son's instruction she practised devotional yoga at Bindusaras, her body withered unnoticed, and she attained the Lord; the place became Siddhapada (Bhāgavata 3.33).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: Daughter of Svāyambhuva Manu, wife of Kardama and mother of Kapila, who asked her son for the path to liberation, received the Kapila Gītā and attained perfection through its yoga (BhP 3.25-33).

name: Devala (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others. The Mahābhārata presents an Asita Devala as teacher of related doctrines; the identity is uncertain.

name: Dēvara Dāsimayya
summary: The weaver-saint (Jēḍara Dāsimayya) of Muddanūru, reckoned by the tradition among the earliest vacanakāras, before Basava; his vacanas, signed Rāmanātha, deny that the self is male or female.

tradition.text: before Basava

scholarly.text: 10th–11th c. (debated; some place him closer to Basava)

notes: Whether 'Dēvara' and 'Jēḍara' Dāsimayya are one person is debated.

name: The Goddess (Devī)
summary: The supreme Goddess, appearing as Bhuvaneśvarī, who teaches Himālaya and the gods in the Devī Gītā (Devī Bhāgavata 7.31-40): she is consciousness, supreme Brahman, whose power is māyā.

name: Dhanapati Sūri
summary: Advaita sub-commentator on Śaṅkara's Gītābhāṣya.

name: Dharma (the god; Yama Dharmarāja)
summary: The deity Dharma, father of Yudhiṣṭhira; he tests his son as the Yakṣa at the lake (3.297–298) and as the dog on the great departure (17.3); Vidura is his incarnation (1.100.28).

name: Dharmadhvaja Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who claims to be liberated while ruling and is tested by the ascetic Sulabhā (12.308).

name: Dharmamegha Āraṇya
summary: Successor of Hariharānanda Āraṇya at the Kāpil Maṭh, Madhupur (recalled; verify).

name: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā (dharmavyādha)
summary: A meat-seller who, living by his inherited work, serving his parents and speaking truth, teaches the brāhmaṇa Kauśika dharma, karma and liberation (3.198–206).
alt_summary: The righteous meat-seller of Mithilā who teaches the proud brāhmaṇa Kauśika the dharma of one's own station and of service to parents (Mahābhārata 3.198-206).

name: Dhṛtarāṣṭra

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: The blind Kuru king, father of Duryodhana; hearer of the Gītā through Sañjaya, of Vidura's counsel (5.33–40), Sanatsujāta's teaching (5.41–45) and Vidura's consolations (11.2–7); he later retires to the forest (Āśramavāsika).

name: Dhruva
summary: Son of King Uttānapāda; slighted by his stepmother, he went to the forest as a child, was initiated by Nārada (BhP 4.8) - or taught by the seven sages (VP 1.11-12) - and by austere meditation on Vāsudeva won the vision of Viṣṇu and the eternal position of the pole-star (dhruva-sthāna).

name: Dinakara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Dinakarī, a commentary on Viśvanātha's Siddhāntamuktāvalī.

name: Dōhara Kakkayya
summary: A leather-worker śaraṇa of 'untouchable' birth honoured among the devotees.

name: Draupadī (Kṛṣṇā, Pāñcālī)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga (the Bhārata war; Kali yuga traditionally from 3102 BCE)

summary: Wife of the Pāṇḍavas; in the forest she questions divine justice and argues for human effort against Yudhiṣṭhira (3.28–33), and after the war urges him to rule (12.14).

name: Duggaḷe
summary: Wife of Dēvara Dāsimayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Durvāsas
summary: The celibate sage whom Śrīkaṇṭha commanded to preserve the Śaiva scripture; he created a mind-born son, Tryambakāditya, and transmitted the secrets to him (Śivadṛṣṭi 7.110-112). Later Kashmirian accounts (Tantrāloka 36; Jayaratha) speak of his three mind-born sons for the non-dual, dual and dual-non-dual teachings, and a 'half' Kaula line - hence the 'three and a half maṭhikās' (TĀ 4.266).
notes: The three-sons account (Tryambaka, Āmardaka, Śrīnātha, plus Ardhatryambaka) is from memory of TĀ 36 and Jayaratha; TĀ 4.266 itself names the Śrī-, Tryambaka-, Ardha- and Āmarda- maṭhikās (confirmed).

name: Ēkānta Rāmayya
summary: The Śaiva devotee of Abalūr who, according to an inscription there, staked his head in a contest with the Jainas, cut it off, offered it to Śiva and received it back.

name: Eknāth
summary: In U06's texts: author of the Eknāthī Bhāgavata, the Marathi commentary on the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata Book 11).

name: Ēkōrāmārādhya
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Kedāra pīṭha (Kedārnāth).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Rāmanātha liṅga at Drākṣārāma and seat name Vairāgya-siṃhāsana: low confidence.

name: Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya
summary: The most prolific Navadvīpa Naiyāyika: the Gādādharī on the Dīdhiti and many vāda treatises, including the Vyutpattivāda and Śaktivāda on verbal cognition.
notes: Teacher relation to Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa is the tradition's account (low confidence).

name: Gaṇeśa (Gajānana)
summary: The elephant-faced lord who, in the Gaṇeśa Purāṇa, teaches King Vareṇya the Gaṇeśa Gītā.

name: Gaṅgāmbike
summary: Basava's wife, daughter of the minister Baladēva; a vacanakāra.

name: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya

scholarly.text: first half of the 14th c. CE

summary: Founder of Navya-Nyāya: his Tattvacintāmaṇi in four books on the four means of knowledge recast Nyāya in a precise technical language.

name: Garuḍa
summary: The eagle-mount of Viṣṇu to whom Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa teaches the Garuḍa Purāṇa; his questions in the Pretakalpa frame the teaching on death and the dead.

name: Gauḍapāda
summary: U09 contribution: a Gauḍapāda is named in the closing verse of the bhāṣya on SK 1–69. Whether he is the Advaita teacher Gauḍapāda (author of the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā, Śaṅkara's paramaguru) is disputed; many scholars regard them as different persons.
notes: Registry id used as mandated; if the merge keeps the two persons apart, the Sāṃkhya commentator should be split out (e.g., tch:gaudapada-samkhya).
alt_summary: In U06's context: a commentary on the Uttara Gītā is ascribed to him (attribution doubtful).

name: Gautama Akṣapāda

tradition.text: an ancient ṛṣi

scholarly.text: the Nyāya Sūtra is usually dated c. 2nd–3rd c. CE; nothing is known of its author(s)

realization_account.text: Called 'the best of sages' (Nyāyavārttika maṅgala) and 'the supremely compassionate sage' who composed the śāstra wishing to lift the world sunk in the mire of pain (Vācaspati, Tātparyaṭīkā on NS 1.1.1).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The sage to whom the Nyāya Sūtra is attributed, the founder of Nyāya. The commentators call him the best of sages who taught the śāstra for the peace of the world.
notes: Popular legends explain 'Akṣapāda' ('eyes in the feet'); not recorded here because the versions could not be checked.

name: Gautamī
summary: An aged brāhmaṇī whose son dies of snakebite; she refuses the vengeance a hunter offers, and in the ensuing debate the serpent, Death and Time each disclaim the cause until karma is named (Anuśāsana 13.1).

name: Govindarāja
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava commentator on the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa (the Bhūṣaṇa).

name: Gūḷūra Siddhavīraṇṇoḍeya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Gummaḷāpurada Siddhaliṅgayati
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Haḍapada Appaṇṇa
summary: The barber śaraṇa, Basava's personal attendant.

name: Haḍapada Liṅgamma
summary: Wife of Haḍapada Appaṇṇa and a vacanakāra.

name: Halageyārya
summary: Compiler of a redaction of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: P. G. Halakatti
summary: Phakīrappa Gurubasappa Halakatti, who collected palm-leaf vacana manuscripts and printed the vacanas from the 1920s, beginning their modern revival ('father of vacana literature' in popular usage).
notes: An editor-publisher rather than a teacher; included as a transmitter of the texts.

name: Haṃsa (the Lord as swan)
summary: The form of a swan in which the Lord appeared before Brahmā and the Kumāras to answer their question (Bhāgavata 11.13.19-42).

name: Hānagal Kumāra Svāmi
summary: Vīraśaiva renunciant who founded the Śivayōga Mandira near Bādāmi (1909) to train virakta ascetics in iṣṭaliṅga yoga, and worked for the community's unity and education.

name: Hanumān
summary: Son of the Wind, Rāma's devoted servant in the Rāmāyaṇa; in the Mahābhārata he meets his brother Bhīma and teaches him the ages of the world and the four sciences — the Veda, economics (vārtā) and polity (daṇḍanīti) (3.147–150).
alt_summary: In the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa the devoted servant judged fit for knowledge, to whom Sītā and Rāma teach the Rāma-hṛdaya (1.1.29-52).

name: Harihara (Kannada poet)
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet of Hampi who created the ragaḷe form for lives of the śaraṇas and of the ancient Śaiva devotees (purātanas), and wrote the Girijākalyāṇa.

name: Hariharānanda Āraṇya
summary: Renunciant who founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur as a monastery of Sāṃkhya-Yoga and lived much of his life in seclusion in a cave there; author of the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga Bhāṣya and of works on Sāṃkhya (e.g., Sāṃkhyatattvāloka), and of the commentary rendered in English as 'Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali'.
notes: Dates, titles and the Maṭh's founding recalled, not checked.
alt_summary: Sāṃkhya-Yoga monk who spent long years in retreat, founded the Kāpil Maṭh at Madhupur, and wrote the Bhāsvatī on the Yoga-bhāṣya and a Bengali exposition of Patañjali's Yoga later published in English.

name: Harirāma Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika of the 17th c., remembered as the teacher of Gadādhara.

name: Hārīta (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Also named in the Māṭhara Vṛtti (on SK 71) among those through whom the knowledge came from Pañcaśikha to Īśvarakṛṣṇa: Bhārgava, Ulūka, Vālmīki, Hārīta, Devala and others.

name: Hayagrīva
summary: The horse-headed form of Viṣṇu (BhP 2.7.11), who in the Lalitopākhyāna is sent as a portion of Viṣṇu to teach Agastya the story and worship of Lalitā.

name: Hemādri

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE, minister at the Yādava court

summary: Author of the Caturvargacintāmaṇi, whose volumes on vows and gifts are the fullest compilation of Purāṇic vrata and dāna.

name: Himavat (Himālaya)
summary: King of the mountains and father of Pārvatī, who asks the Goddess for the yoga, devotion and knowledge that lead to her (Devī Gītā).

name: Hiraṇyadāma

scholarly.text: early 9th c. (as narrated in an inscription of 1052 CE)

summary: Brahmin who, according to the Khmer Sdok Kak Thom inscription (1052 CE), performed rites for King Jayavarman II and taught four Vāma tantras — Vīṇāśikha, Nayottara, Sammoha and Śiraścheda — to the royal priest.

name: Hiraṇyagarbha
alt_names: Pitāmaha (Brahmā) as first teacher of yoga

realization_account.text: The first and most ancient teacher of yoga: 'Hiraṇyagarbha is the speaker of yoga, no other is ancient' (verse cited by Vijñānabhikṣu from the Yoga-Yājñavalkya, YV 1.1). Commentators read 'anuśāsana' in YS 1.1 as Patañjali's re-teaching of the yoga Hiraṇyagarbha taught; Nārāyaṇatīrtha: 'Pitāmaha taught yoga, then Śeṣa'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The tradition's founder of yoga. The Yoga commentators (Vācaspati, Vijñānabhikṣu, Rāmānanda Sarasvatī, Nāgeśa) name Hiraṇyagarbha as the original teacher and treat Patañjali's śāstra as a re-teaching; the Mahābhārata's Nārāyaṇīya likewise pairs Kapila as the teacher of Sāṃkhya with Hiraṇyagarbha as the knower of yoga.
notes: The Mahābhārata reference (Nārāyaṇīya, c. MBh 12.337 CE) and a reported Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā passage on a Hairaṇyagarbha yoga śāstra are from memory and need checking.
alt_summary: Named in the Nārāyaṇīya as the knower (vettā) of Yoga, 'none more ancient' (12.337.60).
alt_notes: U05's contribution; Hiraṇyagarbha as the tradition's founder of Yoga is also treated by U10.

name: Hṛdayaśiva
summary: Compiler of a Prāyaścittasamuccaya of Śaiva expiatory rites.

name: Hṛṣīkeśa Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Palimaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa. He is remembered as the copyist of the manuscript collection of Madhva's works (the Sarvamūla) and as author of the short Sampradāyapaddhati.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Ikṣvāku
summary: First king of the solar dynasty, who received the yoga from Manu; thus the royal sages knew it until it was lost (BhG 4.1–2).

name: Īśānaśiva Gurudeva
summary: Author of the Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, a vast Śaiva ritual compendium (Tantrasāra and Siddhāntasāra) that is a principal authority of Kerala temple tantra.

name: Īśvarakṛṣṇa
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhya Kārikā, who, 'having thoroughly understood the established doctrine handed down by a succession of pupils, summarized it in āryā verses' (SK 71). The Yuktidīpikā says he condensed the Ṣaṣṭitantra out of compassion for pupils of short life. An identification with Vindhyavāsin was proposed by some scholars and is not generally accepted.

name: Jābāli
summary: A brāhmaṇa counsellor who urges Rāma, with arguments that deny the other world, to return and rule; Rāma rejects this, and Vasiṣṭha says Jābāli spoke only to bring Rāma back (Rāmāyaṇa 2.108–110).
notes: Distinct from Satyakāma Jābāla (tch:satyakama-jabala).

name: Jaḍa Bharata

realization_account.text: The king after whom Bhāratavarṣa is named retired to the forest, became attached to an orphaned fawn, died thinking of it and was reborn as a deer; then reborn as a brahmin who, remembering, lived as if dull and dumb, and taught the king of Sindhu-Sauvīra (Rahūgaṇa) the distinction of self and body (BhP 5.7-14; VP 2.13-16).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The exemplar of the power of the last thought (anta-smṛti) and of the avadhūta who hides his realization; teacher of Rahūgaṇa.

name: Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kashmiri poet, author of the Stutikusumāñjali, hymns to Śiva in 38 chapters.

name: Jagadīśa Tarkālaṅkāra
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Jāgadīśī on the Dīdhiti, the Śabdaśaktiprakāśikā and the Tarkāmṛta.

name: Jaigīṣavya

realization_account.text: Through direct perception of his saṃskāras he saw the sequence of his births through ten great creation-cycles, and knowledge born of discrimination arose in him (YBh 3.18).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Ancient yoga master cited in the Yoga-bhāṣya: on mastery of the senses he holds that it is non-apprehension arising from the mind's one-pointedness (YBh 2.55); questioned by Āvaṭya (YBh 3.18), he declares everything he experienced in all births to be suffering, and the unsurpassed happiness of contentment to be suffering compared with the happiness of kaivalya.
notes: The Mahābhārata also tells of Jaigīṣavya (with Asita Devala) — from memory.
alt_summary: A yogin mendicant who, unmoved by praise or blame, teaches Asita Devala equanimity (12.222) and, at a tīrtha on the Sarasvatī, shows Devala his yogic powers, moving unseen between the worlds (9.49).

Sage of Sāṃkhya-Yoga lore. The Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 3.18) records his dialogue with Āvaṭya about the suffering even in the highest births, and cites his view (on YS 2.55) that the highest sense-control is non-apprehension (of objects) through one-pointedness of mind. The Mahābhārata places him in stories with Asita Devala.
alt_notes: The Yoga-bhāṣya's mention of Jaigīṣavya is covered by U10.

name: Jaimini
summary: In the Purāṇas Vyāsa's disciple for the Sāmaveda (VP 3.4), and the questioner of the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa, who asks about the Mahābhārata's puzzles and then about birth, death and liberation. (His identity with the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra author is the traditional view.)

name: Jājali
summary: A proud ascetic, on whose head birds nested while he stood motionless, sent to learn dharma from the merchant Tulādhāra (12.253–256).

name: Janadeva Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā, occupied with the question of what survives death, instructed by Pañcaśikha (12.211–212).

name: Janaka
summary: In U06's texts: King of Videha who receives Aṣṭāvakra's teaching and voices his awakening (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā ch. 2 and later chapters); overhears the Siddhas' songs and awakens (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 5.8-10); his verse 'my wealth is endless, for nothing is mine; if Mithilā burns, nothing of mine burns' is quoted in Mahābhārata 12.171.56.

realization_account.text: On hearing Aṣṭāvakra he exclaims that he is stainless, peaceful consciousness beyond nature, long deceived by delusion (Aṣṭāvakra Gītā 2.1); in the Yoga Vāsiṣṭha he awakens through the Siddha Gītā and rules as one liberated while living.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

name: Janamejaya
summary: Kuru king, great-grandson of Arjuna, at whose snake sacrifice Vaiśampāyana recites the Mahābhārata; his questions open sections such as the discussion of whether puruṣas are many or one (12.338.1).

name: Janārdana Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Krishnapura maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Jātavēdamuni
summary: The teacher under whom, in the hagiographies, Basava studied at Kūḍalasaṅgama.

name: Jayanta Bhaṭṭa
summary: Kashmiri Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyamañjarī, the Nyāyakalikā and the drama Āgamaḍambara, set in the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman (r. 883–902). He defends the Veda and the Lord and examines the validity of the Āgamas.
notes: His son is usually identified as the poet Abhinanda (moderate confidence).

name: Jayaratha
summary: 13th-century Kashmiri scholar, son of Śṛṅgāraratha, author of the Viveka commentary on the whole Tantrāloka - the main source for many lost tantras and for the Mata and Krama - as well as a commentary on the Vāmakeśvarīmata (Śrīvidyā) and a work on poetics.

scholarly.text: 13th c. CE (under King Rājadeva, early 13th c.)

notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue role); U19 owns his exegesis.
alt_summary: Kashmirian commentator on the Tantrāloka whose Viveka preserves, from the lost Śrīkaṇṭhīya Saṃhitā, the catalogues of the 28 Siddhānta tantras and of the 64 Bhairava tantras.

name: Jayatīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1365–1388 in maṭha lists

realization_account.text: The tradition identifies Jayatīrtha with the bull that carried Madhva's manuscripts, who listened to Madhva's teaching and was blessed to become its commentator; seeing the young horseman drink from a river without dismounting, like an animal, Akṣobhya Tīrtha asked what he had been in his past body, and the memory awakened him.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The great commentator (Ṭīkācārya) of the tradition: author of the Nyāyasudhā on the Anuvyākhyāna and the Tattvaprakāśikā on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, commentaries on the Gītā works, the Ṛgbhāṣya and all ten prakaraṇas, and the independent Pramāṇapaddhati and Vādāvalī. His commentaries fixed the scholastic form of Dvaita. In the tradition's account he had been a young cavalryman (Dhoṇḍo Raghunātha of Maṅgaḷavēḍhe) whom Akṣobhya Tīrtha awakened to his past birth.
notes: The location of his brindāvana (Malkheḍ, per the Uttarādi Maṭha; Nava Brindāvana, per another view) is disputed within the tradition — recorded at low confidence. The realization account is oral and hagiographic tradition; no textual source was checked for it.
alt_summary: Author of the Prameyadīpikā and Nyāyadīpikā on Madhva's Gītā works.

name: Jñānanetra (Śivānanda)
summary: Regarded as the founder of the Krama in Kashmir, who received the teaching from the goddess (in Oḍḍiyāna, in the tradition's account) and passed it to three female disciples.
notes: Names of the female disciples (Keyūravatī, Madanikā, Kalyāṇikā) recalled from secondary literature - gap.

name: Jñānaprakāśa
summary: Saiddhāntika author (described as resident of Śālivāṭipura) of a Pauṣkara commentary and of a collection on the greatness and authority of the Śaiva Āgamas.

name: Jñānaśiva
summary: Author of the Jñānaratnāvalī, a compendium of Siddhānta ritual.

name: Jñāneśvar
summary: Author of the Jñāneśvarī, the Marathi verse commentary on the Gītā (1290).
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Kairāta
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa
summary: Vasugupta's disciple, author of the Spandavṛtti and - according to Bhāskara, Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhagavadutpala - of the Spandakārikā itself; his lost Tattvārthacintāmaṇi commented on the last part of the Śiva Sūtra.

scholarly.text: fl. under King Avantivarman (855-883 CE) according to the Rājataraṅgiṇī (5.66)

name: Kaṇāda

tradition.text: an ancient ṛṣi

scholarly.text: the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra core is usually dated around the turn of the era (estimates vary widely)

summary: The sage to whom the Vaiśeṣika Sūtra is attributed, founder of Vaiśeṣika; Praśastapāda salutes him after Īśvara. His names Kaṇabhuj / Kaṇabhakṣa ('grain-eater') are traditionally explained by his living on gleaned grains; Buddhist and Jain sources call the school Aulūkya after his name Ulūka.

name: Kapila

tradition.text: born at the beginning of creation endowed with virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power (Gauḍapāda on SK 1, 43); in the Purāṇic account an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti (Māṭhara on SK 1; Bhāgavata Purāṇa book 3)

realization_account.text: Born with innate (sāṃsiddhika) virtue, knowledge, dispassion and power; seeing the world sunk in blind darkness, out of compassion he taught the knowledge of the twenty-five principles to Āsuri. A saying quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya calls him the first knower who, assuming a created mind (nirmāṇacitta), out of compassion taught the doctrine to the inquiring Āsuri.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Sāṃkhya in the tradition's account: the 'supreme sage' (SK 69) who gave the teaching to Āsuri out of compassion (SK 70). Gauḍapāda counts him among Brahmā's seven mind-born sons; the Māṭhara Vṛtti and the Purāṇas make him an avatāra, son of Kardama and Devahūti. The Sāṃkhya Sūtra and the Tattvasamāsa are ascribed to him; the Mahābhārata and the Bhāgavata Purāṇa (Kapila Gītā) preserve further teachings in his name.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the avatāra Kapila, son of Kardama and Devahūti, who teaches his mother a devotional Sāṃkhya (Kapila Gītā, Bhāgavata 3.25-33). The Bhāgavata identifies him with the founder of Sāṃkhya ('tattva-saṅkhyātā', 3.24-25); some later authors distinguish the two Kapilas.

The Mokṣadharma names Kapila, the supreme seer, as the proclaimer of Sāṃkhya (12.337.60); Nārāyaṇa says the Sāṃkhya teachers call him Kapila (12.326.64); 'among the perfected I am the sage Kapila' (BhG 10.26); in a dialogue Kapila tells Syūmaraśmi that he does not censure the Vedas but that the āśramas' duties have one aim (12.260–262).
In the Bhāgavata the avatāra-teacher of Sāṃkhya, eight-limbed yoga directed to the Lord's form (BhP 3.28) and devotion; a mahājana (6.3.20).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Karāla Janaka
summary: King of Mithilā who questions Vasiṣṭha on the perishable and imperishable and on the knowledge of plurality and unity (12.291–296).

name: Kāśyapa
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Jñānakāṇḍa.

name: Kauṇḍinya (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Distinct from the Pāśupata commentator Kauṇḍinya (tch:kaundinya).

name: Kauśika (the brāhmaṇa of the Vyādha Gītā)
summary: A brāhmaṇa ascetic who burns a crane by his angry glance, is rebuked by a devoted housewife and learns dharma from the meat-seller of Mithilā, then returns to serve his parents (3.196–206).

name: Kavirāja Yati
summary: Renunciant author of the Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpa; its colophon calls him a paramahaṃsa, pupil of Vaikuṇṭha.

name: Keḷadi Basavarāja
summary: Vīraśaiva ruler of Keḷadi (Basavappa Nāyaka) and author of the Sanskrit Śivatattvaratnākara.

name: Keśava Kāśmīrī Bhaṭṭa
summary: Nimbārka-school teacher credited with a Gītā commentary (Tattvaprakāśikā).

name: Keśava Miśra
summary: Author of the Tarkabhāṣā, a primer of syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika.

name: Keśava (Sāṃkhya author)
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyatattvapradīpikā, a short exposition following Vijñānabhikṣu.

name: Keśidhvaja
summary: A Janaka king devoted to knowledge (ātma-vidyā) who, though acting through karma to exhaust it, taught his rival kinsman Khāṇḍikya the nature of ignorance and the eightfold yoga with Viṣṇu as support (VP 6.6-7); he attained liberation by acting without attachment (VP 6.7.105-106).

name: Kētaladēvi
summary: A woman vacanakāra, wife of the potter-devotee Guṇḍayya.

name: Khāṇḍikya Janaka
summary: A Janaka king devoted to ritual action (karma), expelled by Keśidhvaja; asked by him for the expiation for a killed cow, he chose instead to ask for the teaching of yoga, then renounced and dissolved into the Brahman called Viṣṇu (VP 6.6-7.104).

name: Kinnari Bommayya
summary: A śaraṇa remembered as a player of the kinnari lute.

name: Kṛṣṇa (Vāsudeva)

tradition.text: end of the Dvāpara yuga; his departure from the world is taken to begin the Kali yuga (traditionally 3102 BCE)

realization_account.text: The tradition regards him as the Lord (Bhagavān) himself born as Vasudeva's son; in the Gītā he speaks as unborn and imperishable, coming into being by his own māyā (4.6), and the Nārāyaṇīya presents him as a manifestation of Nārāyaṇa.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Son of Vasudeva and Devakī, prince of the Vṛṣṇis, Arjuna's charioteer and teacher of the Bhagavad Gītā and the Anugītā. In the Gītā he speaks as the Lord who descends age after age (4.6–8), is the source of all (10.8) and shows Arjuna his universal form (ch. 11); the Nārāyaṇīya names his birth at Mathurā among Nārāyaṇa's manifestations (12.326.82). In the Anuśāsana he learns the thousand names of Śiva from Upamanyu (13.14–17).
notes: Historicity recorded as 'legendary' in the scholarly sense only; the tradition holds him to be the Lord incarnate.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: speaker of the Uddhava Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.7-29), in which he gives Uddhava his final teaching before leaving the world, and of the Uttara Gītā; he quotes the Kāma Gītā (Mahābhārata 14.13).

name: Kṛṣṇa Mitra
summary: Ācārya named in the colophon of the Sāṃkhya treatise Tattvamīmāṃsā (with his father's and grandfather's names; the e-text reading of the father's name is garbled).

name: Kṣemarāja
summary: Abhinavagupta's foremost disciple; author of the Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya and of commentaries that fused Spanda and Pratyabhijñā and read the Bhairava tantras non-dually: Śivasūtravimarśinī, Spandanirṇaya, Spandasandoha, Svacchandoddyota, Netroddyota, Vijñānabhairavoddyota (incomplete), Stavacintāmaṇivṛtti, Śivastotrāvalīvivṛti, Parāprāveśikā.

name: Lakkaṇṇa Daṇḍēśa
summary: Minister of Dēvarāya II and author of the Kannada Śivatattvacintāmaṇi.

name: Lakṣmaṇa
summary: Rāma's brother: recipient of Rāma's teaching on māyā, knowledge and devotion (Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa 3.4) and of the Rāma Gītā (7.5); in the Rāmcaritmānas he himself teaches Guha (the Lakṣmaṇa Gītā).

name: Lakṣmaṇa Deśika
notes: His identification with Abhinavagupta's teacher Lakṣmaṇagupta is sometimes proposed; not accepted here.
summary: Author of the Śāradātilaka, a manual of mantra-śāstra widely used as an authority, including in Kerala.

name: Lakṣmaṇagupta
summary: Disciple of Utpaladeva and Abhinavagupta's teacher in the Pratyabhijñā; no works survive.

name: Lakṣmīdhara
notes: Contribution from U08 (catalogue role); U23 owns Śrī Vidyā.
summary: Commentator on the Saundaryalaharī from the Samaya standpoint, who rejects the 64 tantras as Kaula and non-Vedic and upholds the five 'auspicious āgamas'.
alt_summary: Author of the Kṛtyakalpataru, the digest that systematised Purāṇic teaching on vows, gifts, tīrthas and śrāddha.

name: Lal Ded (Lalleśvarī, Lallā)
summary: 14th-century Kashmiri yoginī whose vākhs, in the idiom of non-dual Śaivism and yoga, speak of seeking Śiva far and finding him at home in her own body, of breath-practice lighting the lamp of knowledge, and of the indifference of the realized to sectarian names.

realization_account.text: Tradition holds that she left an unhappy married life to wander as an ascetic, dancing unclothed after her teacher's single instruction to turn from the outer to the inner; she is also revered by Kashmiri Muslims (as Lallā Ārifa).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

notes: Her teacher is named in tradition as Siddha Śrīkaṇṭha (Sed Bayu) - low confidence, not given as an id.

name: Laugākṣi Bhāskara
summary: Author of the Tarkakaumudī (Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika) and of the Arthasaṅgraha, a Mīmāṃsā primer.

name: Līlā
summary: Queen who, grieving for her husband Padma, is taught by the goddess Sarasvatī (Jñapti) and shown in consciousness-body the worlds of her husband's past and future lives (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 3.15-60).

name: Lopāmudrā
summary: Agastya's wife and companion in pilgrimage in the Kāśī Khaṇḍa, questioner on tīrthas; in the Śrīvidyā tradition a seer of a form of the Goddess's mantra (U23).

name: Madālasā

realization_account.text: The queen who, under pretext of lulling her crying infants, taught her first sons that the self is pure, that its name is a recent imagination, and that the body of five elements is not theirs (MkP 25.10-18), so that they renounced; she taught Alarka rājadharma and gave him a ring containing a teaching for the time of distress (MkP 26-35).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: A woman teacher of self-knowledge in the Mārkaṇḍeya. Her lullaby opens 'śuddho 'si re tāta, na te 'sti nāma' in the checked e-text (MkP 25.11); the popular verse 'śuddho 'si buddho 'si nirañjano 'si ...' recited under her name was not found there.

name: Mādāra Cennayya
summary: A cobbler (mādāra) devotee of the pre-Basava past whom Basava names as his own household's father ('I am the son in the house of Mādāra Cennayya').
notes: Placement before Basava follows the hagiographies; low confidence.

name: Mādhava Tīrtha
summary: Disciple of Madhva and pontiff after Narahari Tīrtha in the Uttarādi line.

name: Madhusūdana Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Gūḍhārthadīpikā on the Gītā, dividing it into three six-chapter sections on action, devotion and knowledge.
notes: U05's contribution only.

name: Madhuvarasa
summary: A brāhmaṇa śaraṇa (Madhuvayya) who gave his daughter in marriage to Haraḷayya's son and was put to death with him in the tradition's account.

name: Madhva

tradition.text: the tradition's own reckoning: born when 4,300 years of the Kali age had passed (Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya 32.120 = c. 1199 CE) and lived 79 years (to c. 1278); a second traditional reckoning, widely used by the maṭhas, gives 1238–1317

scholarly.text: c. 1238–1317 CE (B. N. K. Sharma, from the epigraphic dates of his disciple Narahari Tīrtha, 1264–1293); some earlier scholars followed 1197/1199–1276/1278

realization_account.text: Madhva is the third avatāra of Vāyu (Mukhyaprāṇa), after Hanumān and Bhīma — he says so himself at the end of the Mahābhārata-tātparya-nirṇaya (32.162, 32.166) and of the Anuvyākhyāna (4.4.15), reading the Balitthā hymn (Ṛgveda 1.141) as naming Vāyu's three forms; Bhīma was reborn as a brāhmaṇa when 4,300 years of Kali had passed to proclaim the truth about Hari hidden by the daityas (MBTN 32.120). The Sumadhvavijaya tells of boyhood feats, renunciation and naming (4.33, 5.1–2), journeys to Badarī where he met Vyāsa and received his teaching, and closes with the gods hailing him as Hanumān, Bhīma and Madhva and showering him with flowers (16.57–58). The tradition holds that he passed from human sight at Uḍupi while expounding the Aitareya Upaniṣad and dwells with Vyāsa at Badarī; the day is kept as Madhva-navamī.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Founder of Dvaita Vedānta (Tattvavāda). Born at Pājaka near Uḍupi to Madhyageha Bhaṭṭa, he took renunciation as a boy from Acyutaprekṣa, receiving the name Pūrṇaprajña (Pūrṇabodha), and was installed as master of Vedānta with the name Ānandatīrtha; he signs his works 'Madhva'. He toured India debating, twice went to Badarī, installed the image of Kṛṣṇa at Uḍupi and founded the eight Uḍupi maṭhas, and wrote thirty-seven works (the Sarvamūla) on the Brahmasūtras, the Gītā, ten Upaniṣads, the Ṛgveda, the epics and Purāṇas, ten polemical and doctrinal treatises, hymns and ritual manuals. He taught that Viṣṇu alone is independent, that the five differences are real and eternal, that souls are graded by nature, and that liberation comes by Viṣṇu's grace through knowledge and devotion.
notes: Scholarly and traditional dates are given in 'dating'. The Uḍupi Kṛṣṇa image is said in the tradition to have come ashore in a block of gopīcandana clay from a ship — not verified in this pass. His mother's name (Vedavatī in later tradition) was not found in the Sumadhvavijaya e-text by a simple search.
alt_summary: Author of a Gītā commentary and the Gītātātparyanirṇaya, and of the Mahābhāratatātparyanirṇaya, reading the epic as proclaiming Viṣṇu's supremacy.

name: Maḍivāḷa Mācayya
summary: The washerman śaraṇa of Kalyāṇa, remembered as the fierce defender of the devotees (gaṇācāra) who protected the śaraṇas and their vacana bundles in the flight after the upheaval.

name: Mahādeva Vedāntin
summary: Author of the Sāṃkhyasūtravṛttisāra, a commentary on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra largely abridging Aniruddha.

name: Mahādevabhaṭṭa
summary: Disciple of Prajñārjuna in Bhāskara's lineage (Vārttika 1.7).

name: Mohandas K. Gandhi
summary: Leader who called the Gītā his 'mother' and read it as teaching action without attachment to fruits (anāsakti) and non-violence; author of Anāsakti Yoga.
notes: Recent (post-1800); no initiatory lineage — lineage field records the text-tradition he interpreted.

name: Maheśacandra Nyāyaratna
summary: Calcutta Sanskrit scholar (principal of the Sanskrit College), author of the Navyanyāyabhāṣāpradīpa, a guide to the technical terms of Navya-Nyāya.

name: Maheśvarānanda
summary: South Indian (Cola country) teacher of the Krama (Mahārtha) around 1300, disciple of Mahāprakāśa; author of the Prakrit Mahārthamañjarī with the Sanskrit Parimala, synthesizing Krama, Pratyabhijñā and Śrīvidyā.
notes: Teacher's name Mahāprakāśa and alias Gorakṣa from memory (low).

name: Maitreya (sage)
summary: The sage who questions Parāśara in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa (VP 1.1.1-11) and who, in the Bhāgavata's third and fourth books, instructs Vidura on creation and the Lord's deeds. Not the Buddhist Maitreya.

name: Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya
summary: Andhra Śaiva teacher contemporary with Basava, founder figure of the Ārādhya Śaivas and subject of Pālkuriki Sōmanātha's Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra.

name: Maṇikaṇṭha Miśra
summary: Pre-Gaṅgeśa Naiyāyika, author of the Nyāyaratna.

name: Maṅki
summary: A man who, after losing his young bulls, renounces desire and speaks the Maṅki Gītā (12.171).
alt_summary: Singer of the Maṅki Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.171), who renounced desire after his efforts at wealth failed. A Maṅki is also taught by Vasiṣṭha in the Mokṣopāya's Nirvāṇa book (MU 6.180-183; identity of the two not asserted).

name: Manu Vaivasvata
summary: Son of Vivasvat, who received the yoga from him and passed it to Ikṣvāku (BhG 4.1).
notes: Distinguished from Svāyambhuva Manu, to whom the Manusmṛti is ascribed.

name: Marīci
notes: Contribution from U08 (Vaikhānasa role).
summary: Disciple of Vikhanas to whom the Vaikhānasa tradition ascribes the Vimānārcanakalpa.

name: Maritoṇṭadārya
summary: Author of the Tattvapradīpikā commentary on the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi and of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā.

name: Mārkaṇḍeya
summary: The long-lived sage who instructs the Pāṇḍavas in the forest (3.180–221): on karma, the ages and the dissolution — in which he saw the worlds within the body of a divine child on a banyan branch (3.186.81–91) — the devoted wife and the righteous meat-seller.

realization_account.text: The long-lived sage who, by Nara-Nārāyaṇa's boon, witnessed an illusory deluge and saw the Lord as an infant lying on a banyan leaf, entering and leaving the child's body (BhP 12.8-10).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: The ever-young sage in whose name the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa is told; he directs Jaimini to the wise birds and narrates the Devī Māhātmya as the story of the eighth Manu.

name: Maruḷārādhya (Maruḷasiddha)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Ujjayinī pīṭha (Ujjaini, Kūḍligi taluk, Karnataka).

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Seat name Saddharma-siṃhāsana (low confidence).

name: Māṭhara
summary: Commentator on the SK named in the colophon of the Māṭhara Vṛtti; his date is disputed.

name: Mathurānātha Tarkavāgīśa
summary: Navadvīpa Naiyāyika, author of the Rahasya commentaries (Māthurī) on the Tattvacintāmaṇi, the Dīdhiti and Udayana's works.

name: Maunappa Paṇḍita
summary: Author of the Vīraśaivācārakaustubha.

name: Māyidēva
summary: Author ascribed the Sanskrit Anubhavasūtra on the ṣaṭsthala path.

name: Medhas
summary: The brahmin sage (dvijavarya, MkP 81.9) in whose forest hermitage the Devī Māhātmya is taught to the deposed king Suratha and the merchant Samādhi.

name: Medhāvin
summary: The son in the father–son dialogue of the Mokṣadharma (12.169), who urges his father to seek the self now because death is always near.

name: Mōḷige Mahādēvi
summary: Wife of Mōḷige Mārayya and a vacanakāra.

name: Mōḷige Mārayya
summary: A king (Kashmir in the tradition's account) who renounced his kingdom and lived in Kalyāṇa by selling bundles of firewood (mōḷige).

name: Muddadeva
summary: An ācārya of the Śivayogin lineage from which the Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi's author descends; named Muddadeva because he gave joy (mud) to all beings (SSM 1.15–16).

name: Muḍumba Narasiṃhasvāmin
summary: Author to whom the Sāṃkhyataruvasanta, a late commentary on the SK, is ascribed.

name: Mūka (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Muktananda
summary: In U06's context (recent reception): made the Guru Gītā the daily morning chant of his ashrams (Ganeshpuri recension).

name: Muktāyakka
summary: The woman śaraṇa who, grieving her brother Ajagaṇṇa, was met by Allama; their exchange on grief, speech and silence is a chapter of the Śūnyasampādane.

name: Naciketas
summary: In U06's texts: the addressee of the Agni Purāṇa's Yama Gītā, which retells the Kaṭha Upaniṣad teaching.

name: Nāgeśa Bhaṭṭa
summary: Pāṇinian grammarian (Laghuśabdenduśekhara, Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntamañjūṣā) who also wrote a vṛtti on the Yoga Sūtra.
alt_summary: U09 contribution: the grammarian Nāgeśa of Vārāṇasī, to whom a short vṛtti on the Sāṃkhya Sūtra is ascribed (low confidence).

name: Nahuṣa
summary: Ancient king cursed to be a python; he seizes Bhīma and is freed when Yudhiṣṭhira answers his questions on who is a brāhmaṇa (3.173–178).

name: Nandikeśvara (author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā)
summary: Vīraśaiva author of the Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā defending the wearing of the liṅga.
notes: Distinct from the mythic Nandikeśvara and from the authors on grammar and dance of that name.

name: Nārada

realization_account.text: In a former life the son of a maidservant who served Vedāntin sages, heard Hari's glories, had a vision of the Lord and was told he would see him again only in a later body (BhP 1.5.23-1.6.38); reborn as the celestial sage who wanders singing Hari's names with his vīṇā. BhP 1.3.8 counts him the third avatāra, who 'expounded the Sātvata tantra'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The divine sage and wandering devotee: teacher of Vyāsa (urging him to write the Bhāgavata), initiator of Dhruva with the twelve-syllable mantra, teacher of Prahlāda while still in his mother's womb, pupil of the Kumāras in the Nārada Purāṇa; one of the twelve mahājanas (BhP 6.3.20).
alt_summary: Divine seer; in the Nārāyaṇīya he visits Nara and Nārāyaṇa at Badarī and the White Island, where Nārāyaṇa shows himself and teaches him (12.321–339); he asks Asita Devala about the origin of beings (12.267) and relates the origin of Death (12.248–250); he tells Vālmīki the story of Rāma (Rāmāyaṇa 1.1). 'Among divine seers I am Nārada' (BhG 10.26).
Divine sage who, in Pāñcarātra texts, receives the teaching — from Ahirbudhnya in the Ahirbudhnya Saṃhitā and from Bhagavān in the Jayākhya.
notes: U05's contribution; the Nārada Bhakti Sūtra is covered by U25.
alt_notes: Contribution from U08 (Pāñcarātra role); other units record his other roles.

name: Narahari Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1324–1333 in maṭha lists

scholarly.text: his inscriptions at Śrīkūrmam are dated c. 1264–1293 CE

summary: Disciple of Madhva and his successor after Padmanābha Tīrtha in the Uttarādi line. The tradition says he had served as regent of the Kaliṅga kingdom and brought from its treasury the images of Rāma and Sītā (Mūla Rāma) that Madhva had asked for; inscriptions of his at Śrīkūrmam are used by scholars to date Madhva.
notes: The tradition also credits him with fostering Yakṣagāna — low confidence, not verified.

name: Narasiṃha Tīrtha (Adamaru)
summary: Disciple of Madhva and, in the tradition's account, founder of the Adamaru maṭha, one of the eight maṭhas of Uḍupi that take turns in the worship of Kṛṣṇa.
notes: Founder-to-maṭha assignment recalled from memory; check against maṭha records.

name: Narasiṃhagupta (Cukhulaka)
summary: Abhinavagupta's father and his first teacher (in grammar), named by Abhinavagupta in the Tantrāloka's closing chapter.

name: Nārāyaṇa
summary: In the Nārāyaṇīya the supreme Lord, also present as the ṛṣi Nārāyaṇa who with Nara performs austerity at Badarī (both born in Dharma's house, 12.332.19); he shows himself to Nārada in the White Island and teaches the fourfold form, his manifestations and the ekāntin dharma (12.321–339).

name: Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya
summary: Son of Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya and author of the Sumadhvavijaya, the principal life of Madhva, of the Maṇimañjarī and of the Yogadīpikā, a manual of worship and meditation.
notes: Authorship of all three works as named in their colophons in the raw_etexts corpus.

name: Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha
summary: U09 contribution: author to whom the Sāṃkhyacandrikā on the SK is ascribed; several authors share the name, and identifications are uncertain.

name: Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha
summary: Kashmirian Saiddhāntika who wrote the Vṛtti on the Mṛgendra, defending a dualist reading of the scripture; father of Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha.

name: Nārāyaṇatīrtha
summary: Author of two commentaries on the Yoga Sūtra, the Yogasiddhāntacandrikā and the Sūtrārthabodhinī; a devotee of Kṛṣṇa who interprets Yoga within Vedānta and subsumes many named yogas under the eight-limbed yoga.
notes: Identity with Nārāyaṇa Tīrtha, composer of the Kṛṣṇalīlātaraṅgiṇī, is sometimes asserted — not verified.

name: Nidāgha
summary: Son of Pulastya and disciple of Ṛbhu, who lived at Vīranagara on the Devikā; Ṛbhu returns twice in disguise to test and teach him (Viṣṇu Purāṇa 2.15-16); the recipient of the Ṛbhu Gītā.
alt_summary: Pulastya's son and Ṛbhu's disciple, visited by his teacher twice in disguise and brought to see that there is no difference between 'king' and 'elephant', 'I' and 'you' (VP 2.15-16).

name: Nijaguṇa Śivayōgi
summary: Vīraśaiva yogin and author of the Kannada encyclopaedia Vivekacintāmaṇi and of the songs of the Kaivalya Paddhati.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara
summary: Seventeenth-century Mahārāṣṭrian scholar in Vārāṇasī, famous for his Mahābhārata commentary; in U06 the commentator on the Gaṇeśa Gītā.
alt_summary: Maharashtrian scholar at Vārāṇasī, author of the Bhāratabhāvadīpa, the commentary on the whole Mahābhārata that fixed the vulgate text.

name: Nīlakaṇṭha (author of the Kriyāsāra)
summary: Author of the Sanskrit Vīraśaiva Kriyāsāra.

name: Nīlāmbike
summary: Basava's wife and a vacanakāra in whose vacanas Basava appears as her spiritual guide.

name: Niṣkriyānandanātha
summary: Krama master named in Anantaśaktipāda's commentary on the Vātūlanāthasūtra as having received instruction from the siddhas of Gandhamādana; the Chummāsaṅketaprakāśa is ascribed to him.

name: Nuliya Candayya
summary: The rope-maker śaraṇa remembered for insisting that kāyaka is not to be interrupted even for worship.

name: Padmanābha Tīrtha

tradition.text: pontificate c. 1317–1324 in maṭha lists

summary: Disciple of Madhva and first pontiff after him in the line that became the Uttarādi Maṭha; author of the Sattarkadīpāvalī (on the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya) and Nyāyaratnāvalī (on the Anuvyākhyāna). In the tradition's account he had been a learned opponent (named Śobhana Bhaṭṭa) before becoming Madhva's disciple.
notes: Former name, pontificate dates and brindāvana location recalled at low confidence.

name: Pakṣadhara Miśra
summary: Mithilā Naiyāyika, also called Jayadeva, author of the Āloka commentary on the Tattvacintāmaṇi.
notes: Tradition makes him the Mithilā master whom Raghunātha Śiromaṇi challenged (low confidence).

name: Pālkuriki Sōmanātha
summary: Telugu and Kannada Vīraśaiva poet-scholar, author of the Basava Purāṇamu, the Paṇḍitārādhya Caritra and the Vṛṣādhipa Śatakamu.

name: Pañcādhikaraṇa
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher known from the Yuktidīpikā: the organs are elemental (bhautika); the instrument is by nature empty, like a deserted village or dry river bed, its knowledges coming from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from another'; a permanent conveying (ātivāhika) subtle body enters the embryo; knowledge is natural (at the same time as the principles, innate, or flowing) or acquired. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Pañcaśikha
summary: Pupil of Āsuri by whom 'the doctrine was expanded' (SK 70). In the Mahābhārata's Mokṣadharma he teaches King Janaka (Janadeva) of Mithilā. Sayings ascribed to him are quoted in the Yoga Bhāṣya (on YS 1.4, 1.25, 1.36, 2.13, as identified by Vācaspati Miśra) and in the Tattvakaumudī on SK 2; the Sāṃkhya Sūtra cites his views by name (5.32, 6.68).
notes: Mahābhārata chapter (Śāntiparvan, c. 12.211–212 in the critical edition) recalled, not checked.
alt_summary: In the Mokṣadharma, Pañcaśikha 'Kāpileya' (so called because the brāhmaṇī Kapilā nursed him), 'Āsuri's first disciple', comes to Mithilā and so impresses king Janadeva Janaka that he leaves a hundred teachers to follow him (12.211.6–18); he teaches the Sāṃkhya discrimination (12.211–212); Sulabhā refers to Janaka's having learned from him (12.308).

name: Paṇḍitārādhya (of the five ācāryas)
summary: One of the five ācāryas of the Pañcācārya tradition, founder in its account of the Śrīśaila pīṭha.

tradition.text: appears in every yuga under different names

notes: Emergence from the Mallikārjuna liṅga at Śrīśaila and seat name Sūrya-siṃhāsana: low confidence. Distinct entry from the historical Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya (tch:mallikarjuna-panditaradhya); some accounts connect them.

name: Paramārtha
summary: Indian Buddhist monk-translator who reached China in 546. Besides Yogācāra works he translated the Sāṃkhya Kārikā with a commentary (Jin qishi lun) and wrote a Life of Vasubandhu that tells of the Sāṃkhya master Vindhyavāsa's debate with Buddhamitra.

name: Parāśara
summary: Grandson of Vasiṣṭha and father of Vyāsa; the speaker of the Viṣṇu Purāṇa to Maitreya, which he received from Vasiṣṭha and Pulastya after renouncing his rite to burn the rākṣasas (VP 1.1.12-26).
alt_summary: Seer, father of Vyāsa; he instructs king Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (12.279–287).
In U06's texts: the sage who instructs King Janaka in the Parāśara Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.279-287).
notes: U05's contribution (the epic account).

name: Parāśara Bhaṭṭar
summary: Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher, son of Kūrattāḻvāṉ, author of the Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa on the Viṣṇu Sahasranāma.

name: Parīkṣit
summary: Grandson of Arjuna, protected in the womb by Kṛṣṇa; cursed to die in seven days, he renounced his kingdom and sat in prāyopaveśa on the Gaṅgā (BhP 1.19), where he heard the Bhāgavata from Śuka; the model hearer (śravaṇa) of the Purāṇa. He also subdued Kali and assigned him five places (BhP 1.17).

name: Pārvatī
summary: Śiva's consort, the questioner in the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa (her doubt why the supreme Rāma grieved for Sītā, 1.1.13-15) and in the Guru Gītā; in Śākta texts identified with the Goddess who herself teaches (Devī Gītā, Bhagavatī Gītā).

name: Patañjali
alt_names: Śeṣa / Ananta (as whose incarnation he is regarded)

tradition.text: not dated by the tradition (incarnation of Śeṣa); identified with the grammarian

scholarly.text: c. 325–425 CE if author of the Pātañjala Yogaśāstra (Maas); the grammarian Patañjali is dated c. 2nd c. BCE

realization_account.text: Regarded as an incarnation of Śeṣa (Ananta), the serpent of Viṣṇu, who took a human form out of compassion to teach; the bhāṣya's maṅgala verse praises the 'lord of serpents, giver of yoga'. Later tradition credits him with removing the impurities of speech (grammar), mind (yoga) and body (medicine) — Bhoja's introductory verses praise Bhoja for doing the same 'like the lord of serpents'.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Author (re-teacher) of the Yoga Sūtra. The tradition regards him as Śeṣa incarnate and as the same Patañjali who wrote the grammatical Mahābhāṣya; modern scholarship mostly distinguishes the two and debates whether he also wrote the bhāṣya (the 'Pātañjala Yogaśāstra' hypothesis).

name: Patañjali (Sāṃkhya teacher)
summary: A Sāṃkhya teacher cited by the Yuktidīpikā: mahat arises directly from pradhāna; all transformation of the organs is 'from itself'; subtle bodies arise and cease repeatedly (one leads the organs to the womb, another arises at death). Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others). Whether he is the author of the Yoga Sūtra (tch:patanjali) is disputed.

name: Paurika
summary: Sāṃkhya teacher who held, according to the Yuktidīpikā (on SK 56), that each puruṣa has its own pradhāna producing its body and the rest; when the pradhāna of the great-bodied one (māhātmyaśarīra) operates, the others operate, and when it ceases, they cease. The Yuktidīpikā rejects this for want of proof. Named in the Yuktidīpikā's list of teachers through whom the doctrine passed between Pañcaśikha and Īśvarakṛṣṇa (on SK 71: Hārīta, Vāddhali, Kairāta, Paurika, Ṛṣabheśvara, Pañcādhikaraṇa, Patañjali, Vārṣagaṇya, Kauṇḍinya, Mūka and others).

name: Piṅgalā
summary: A courtesan of Videha whose sudden disenchantment while waiting for clients makes her one of the avadhūta's teachers (Bhāgavata 11.8.22-44) and the singer of the Piṅgalā Gītā (Mahābhārata 12.168.46-52): 'hope is the greatest misery, hopelessness the greatest happiness'.

realization_account.text: Waiting through the night for a rich lover, she felt deep disgust, turned to the Self as her true beloved and slept happily, free of expectation.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

alt_summary: A courtesan who, waiting in vain for a lover, gave up hope and slept happily; her saying 'freedom from hope is the highest happiness' is quoted in the Mokṣadharma (12.168.52).

name: Pradyumnabhaṭṭa
summary: Kallaṭa's maternal cousin (mātuleya), to whom he transmitted the secret teaching of the Śiva Sūtra (Bhāskara, Vārttika 1.6).

name: Prahlāda

realization_account.text: Son of the demon-king Hiraṇyakaśipu, devoted to Viṣṇu from the womb; unharmed by his father's attempts to kill him; saved by Narasiṃha; refuses boons and liberation for himself alone (BhP 7.4-10; VP 1.16-20).
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: The child-devotee who taught his demon schoolfellows the nine forms of devotion (BhP 7.5.23-24) and that devotion should be practised from childhood (7.6.1); a mahājana (6.3.20) and king of the daityas in Sutala.
alt_summary: In U06's texts: the asura king who realizes the Self through his own inquiry and Viṣṇu's grace and remains in long samādhi until awakened by Viṣṇu to rule (Yoga Vāsiṣṭha 5.30-43); he questions the python-vow sage (Mahābhārata 12.172).

Daitya king; in the Mokṣadharma he explains to Indra that all states arise and cease by their own nature (svabhāva), so pride and grief are baseless (12.215), and questions a sage living like a python (12.172).

name: Prajñārjuna
summary: Son and disciple of Pradyumnabhaṭṭa in Bhāskara's lineage (Vārttika 1.6-7).

name: Praśastapāda
summary: Author of the Padārthadharmasaṅgraha, which gave Vaiśeṣika its classical form: six categories, twenty-four qualities, creation and dissolution by Maheśvara's will, and a systematic theory of cognition and dharma.

name: Purūravas (Aila)
summary: King, son of Iḍā, infatuated with the apsaras Urvaśī; his song of disenchantment is the Aila Gītā (Bhāgavata 11.26).

name: Rāghavabhaṭṭa
summary: Author of the Padārthādarśa (1493/94), a learned commentary on the Śāradātilaka.

name: Rāghavānanda Sarasvatī
summary: Author of the Pātañjalarahasya, a gloss on Vācaspati's Tattvavaiśāradī.

name: Rāghavāṅka
summary: Kannada Vīraśaiva poet, nephew and disciple of Harihara, author of the Hariścandra Kāvya, the Siddharāma Cāritra and the Sōmanātha Cāritra.

name: Rāghavendra Tīrtha

tradition.text: entered his brindāvana at Mantrālaya in 1671

realization_account.text: The tradition holds that Rāghavendra was Prahlāda reborn (through Bāhlīka and Vyāsatīrtha), that he entered his brindāvana alive in 1671, and that he remains present there, answering devotees.
realization_account.label: the tradition's account

summary: Born Veṅkaṭanātha at Bhuvanagiri, disciple of Sudhīndra Tīrtha, and author of the Parimala on the Nyāyasudhā (hence 'Parimalācārya'), the Bhāvadīpa on the Tattvaprakāśikā, the Tantradīpikā, the Nyāyamuktāvalī, the Candrikāprakāśa, the Bhāṭṭasaṅgraha on Mīmāṃsā, Upaniṣad khaṇḍārthas and the Gītāvivṛti. His brindāvana at Mantrālaya is the tradition's greatest pilgrimage centre.
notes: The claim that he will remain in the brindāvana for 700 years is recalled at low confidence.

name: Raghudeva Nyāyālaṅkāra
summary: Navya-Naiyāyika to whom a set of vāda treatises (Muktivāda, Īśvaravāda, Prāgabhāvavāda, Ākāṅkṣāvāda, Sāmagrīvāda and others) is attributed in their modern edition.

name: Raghunātha Śiromaṇi
summary: Founder of the Navadvīpa school of Navya-Nyāya; his Dīdhiti on the Tattvacintāmaṇi became the base of later study, and his Padārthatattvanirūpaṇa re-examined the list of categories.
notes: The tradition tells of his defeating Pakṣadhara in debate in Mithilā (low confidence).

name: Raghūttama Tīrtha
